title: Let's Thank Universal Pictures for Monster Movies!
summary: Josh, Chuck and Jerry Gould-Roland open October with casual talk about recent horror movies, then trace the history of Universal's classic monster movies. They cover Universal's founding by Carl Laemmle and its early star-system publicity, the 1920s precursors (Hunchback of Notre Dame, Phantom of the Opera with Lon Chaney Sr.), and the 1931 Dracula with Bela Lugosi and Frankenstein with Boris Karloff, plus James Whale's Bride of Frankenstein and The Invisible Man. Further segments cover the 1932 Mummy, Poe adaptations, the 1934 Black Cat, the Wolf Man, the studio's financial trouble and sale to Standard Capital, 1940s monster rallies and Abbott and Costello crossovers, Lugosi's decline and Plan 9, 1950s Creature from the Black Lagoon and Millicent Patrick, 1960s-70s revivals (Hammer, Blackula, Groovy Ghoulies, Young Frankenstein), 1990s-2010s revivals (The Mummy 1999, Van Helsing, the cancelled Dark Universe, The Invisible Man 2020, The Shape of Water). The episode closes with a listener mail about Jamaican sound systems.

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Show opening and iHeart intro.

segments.title: Opening banter on October and recent horror movies
segments.summary: The hosts open October and chat about recent horror films they watched, including Backrooms, Undertone, Martyrs and The Devil's Bath.

segments.title: Universal monsters and early horror films
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Universal monster movies of the 1930s as a kickoff for monster films. Chuck notes Caligari and Nosferatu in the early 1920s as earlier horror films.

segments.title: Carl Laemmle and the founding of Universal
segments.summary: Carl Laemmle, a German immigrant, opened a Nickelodeon in Chicago, founded the Independent Motion Picture Company, merged companies into Universal Pictures in 1912, and opened a 230-acre Los Angeles studio in 1915. The hosts discuss the Big Five studios of the time.

segments.title: Florence Lawrence and the star system
segments.summary: Laemmle launched a publicity campaign around actress Florence Lawrence, including a fake car-crash death story blamed on Biograph, helping start the star system.

segments.title: Early Universal horror: Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, Hunchback, Phantom
segments.summary: Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde (1913) is considered Universal's first monster film but is only 26 minutes long. The 1923 Hunchback of Notre Dame and 1925 Phantom of the Opera starred Lon Chaney Sr., the man of a thousand faces.

segments.title: Lon Chaney Sr. and makeup
segments.summary: Lon Chaney Sr. appeared in many films, did his own makeup, and reportedly wrote the Encyclopedia Britannica makeup entry.

segments.title: Dracula 1931 and Bela Lugosi casting
segments.summary: Dracula premiered on Valentine's Day 1931, marketed as a romance, directed by Todd Browning after Lon Chaney Sr. died in 1930. Bela Lugosi, who had starred in the Broadway stage adaptation, was cast. The film was not authorized by Stoker's estate, which the hosts note regarding Nosferatu.

segments.title: Watching old films and Spanish-language Dracula
segments.summary: Josh says he watched Dracula, Bride of Frankenstein and The Invisible Man for the first time. The hosts discuss how 1930s black-and-white films look. They describe the Spanish-language Dracula shot at night by George Melford on the same sets, and how the Hays Code led to cuts.

segments.title: Frankenstein 1931 and James Whale
segments.summary: Frankenstein, released Thanksgiving 1931 and directed by James Whale, is discussed along with Whale's style, the film Gods and Monsters, and the influence of German cinema. The Invisible Man's effects are praised.

segments.title: Monster tropes and Bride of Frankenstein
segments.summary: The hosts discuss monster film tropes such as the mad scientist lab and the hunchback assistant, and Igor's later introduction in 1939. Bride of Frankenstein has the monster learn to talk.

segments.title: Bride of Frankenstein and The Bride (2026)
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the camp and queer-coded character Dr. Pretorius in Bride of Frankenstein, then briefly compare with Maggie Gyllenhaal's The Bride.

segments.title: The Mummy 1932 and Egypt fever
segments.summary: The first Mummy film came out in 1932, about ten years after Tutankhamun's tomb was opened, reflecting Egypt fever. Karloff played a high priest reanimated in modern times, wearing a fez.

segments.title: Universal horror films of the early 1930s
segments.summary: Frankenstein was reportedly the top-grossing film of 1931. Other titles include Murders in the Rue Morgue (1932), White Zombie (1932, independent shot on Universal stages, Lugosi), and its zombie tropes based on W.B. Seabrook's The Magic Island.

segments.title: Poe adaptations, The Black Cat and the Wolf Man
segments.summary: The Black Cat (1934) was a Poe adaptation and first pairing of Lugosi and Karloff. The Invisible Man (1933) was based on H.G. Wells. The Werewolf of London (1935) preceded The Wolf Man (1941) starring Lon Chaney Jr.

segments.title: Studio finances and sale to Standard Capital
segments.summary: Carl Laemmle Jr. ran the studio, spent heavily, including on Show Boat, which was a hit but left the studio in arrears. Laemmle Sr. had used the studio as loan collateral; Standard Capital bought Universal after missed payments and Laemmle Jr. resigned.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break and return from break; discussion of the Regina Wiltshire Theater.

segments.title: 1938 revival and monster rallies
segments.summary: The 1938 Regina Wiltshire Theater revived monster movies to smash success, prompting new monster films and Lugosi returning to work. The 1940s monster rallies included Frankenstein Meets the Wolf Man (1943) and House of Frankenstein (1944).

segments.title: Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein
segments.summary: The 1948 comedy Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein featured Dracula, the Wolf Man and the Invisible Man, and the hosts say the crossovers signaled the franchise jumping the shark.

segments.title: Lugosi's decline, Plan 9 and Ed Wood
segments.summary: Bela Lugosi hit hard times; his last film was Plan 9 from Outer Space, and he died during filming. He was buried in his Dracula cape. The hosts recommend Tim Burton's Ed Wood and the Bauhaus song Bela Lugosi's Dead.

segments.title: Off-topic banter
segments.summary: Brief tangent on Tim Burton films and the Beetlejuice sequel.

segments.title: Creature from the Black Lagoon and Millicent Patrick
segments.summary: The 1954 Creature from the Black Lagoon, a 3D film, is discussed. Millicent Patrick designed the Gill-man suit, though Bud Westmore took credit. Revenge of the Creature featured Clint Eastwood in a bit part and was the first MST3K episode with Bill Corbett as Crow.

segments.title: 1960s shift and monster pop culture
segments.summary: Universal moved toward romantic comedies in the 1960s while the monsters lived on in TV reruns and hosts like Vampira and Elvira. Boris Karloff sang Monster Mash, and appeared on Shindig; he also voiced How the Grinch Stole Christmas.

segments.title: Hammer, Dracula crossovers, Blackula and Groovy Ghoulies
segments.summary: Hammer Film Productions made color versions with Christopher Lee and Peter Cushing, including Satanic Rites of Dracula and The Legend of the Seven Vampires with the Shaw Brothers. Western mashups and Blackula (1972) are mentioned. Groovy Ghoulies (1970) and monster model kits are recalled.

segments.title: Young Frankenstein and 1979 Dracula
segments.summary: Mel Brooks' Young Frankenstein (1974) and Frank Langella's Dracula (1979) are mentioned as notable entries.

segments.title: Revivals: The Mummy 1999, Van Helsing, Wolf Man 2010, Dark Universe, Invisible Man 2020, Shape of Water
segments.summary: After slashers dominated the 1980s, The Mummy (1999) was a smash. Van Helsing (2004) and The Wolfman (2010) followed. The planned Dark Universe with Johnny Depp, Angelina Jolie and Javier Bardem was scrapped after Tom Cruise's 2017 Mummy flopped. The 2020 Invisible Man with Elizabeth Moss is praised; The Shape of Water and del Toro's Frankenstein are discussed.

segments.title: Closing thoughts on Universal monsters
segments.summary: The hosts recommend watching The Invisible Man and old movies and sign off on the monster episode.

segments.title: Listener mail: Maritone Music sound system
segments.summary: Listener Roger Blake writes that his paternal grandfather started Maritone Music, a Jamaican sound system in the 1950s that recently celebrated its 75th anniversary, in response to the August 6 reggae episode. The hosts invite listeners to send ancestor stories.
